# Project Kestrel — Seller Document Review: Departures from Buyer Playbook & Recommended Pushback

I have reviewed the Seller’s updated SPA positions and Disclosure Letter against our internal buyer playbook. Several significant departures from our agreed negotiating position are apparent. Below is my assessment, item by item, with reasoning and recommendations.

---

## 1. General Liability Cap: 20% / AUD 4,800,000 with De Minimis AUD 25,000 & Basket AUD 250,000

**Playbook position:** Starting cap 25% / AUD 6,000,000; conditional fallback at 20% requires **prior written authority from Amelia Frost** identifying the draft; de minimis AUD 5,000; aggregate basket AUD 50,000, seller liable from the first dollar once exceeded.

**Seller offers:** 20% / AUD 4,800,000 as the (essentially) agreed cap; de minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000.

**Assessment.** The cap level itself may be acceptable as a renegotiated target depending on the current evidence picture, but three problems remain:

- **(a) No Amelia Frost pre-approval.** Our playbook expressly conditions the 20% cap on prior written authority from the buyer principal. The Seller treats 20% as unconditional. This is a direct departure — if the buyer later wishes to escalate, it cannot do so without documented approval. We should insist on either accepting 20% with a **documented limitation** (or amending the SPA to reflect an internal note) or declining to negotiate and walking back to 25%.
- **(b) De minimis and basket dramatically lower than our thresholds.** AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 basket would allow claims as small as AUD 250,000 ($2.5k excess) and even lower in amount, well below the AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 floor. From a risk-management perspective this is poor for the buyer — many legitimate small claims could fall inside the "off-limit" zone. We should push back on raising de minimis to AUD 5,000 and the basket to AUD 50,000, at minimum, unless we secure the Amelia Frost override for the lower caps.

**Recommendation.** Raise the baskets to at least AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000. On the 20% cap, either (i) accept with a clean amendment stating it was negotiated with prior Amelia Frost authorisation, or (ii) decline to negotiate and revert to 25%. Do not accept as-is.

---

## 2. Time Limits: 18 Months after Completion

**Playbook position:** 24 months standard; 18 months is a **fallback requiring Amelia Frost written approval** (none given).

**Seller proposes:** 18 months general claim period; limitations apply to all Claims of any nature.

**Assessment.** The Seller collapses all time limits to 18 months and applies them indiscriminately. This is our largest single issue. An 18-month window — especially one extending over and beyond the standard 24 months — may eliminate claims arising within the first year post-closing or those tied to ongoing duties. The Seller's attempt to extend the "limitation" regime to Title/capacity claims further (see below) compounds this.

**Recommendation.** Reject the 18-month period outright (unless we can simultaneously secure Amelia Frost approval for the fallback, which we cannot based on current standing). Restore 24 months. If the Seller insists, require a split: 24 months for general claims and 12 months (or longer, at seller's risk) for Title/capacity.

---

## 3. Fundamental / Title Claims Subject to Same Caps and 18-Month Window

**Playbook position:** Separate regime, **100% cap**, at least six years, outside the general basket/de minimis/knowledge bar.

**Seller proposes:** Capacity and title warranties be subject to the same 20% cap and 18-month window.

**Assessment.** This directly contradicts our single most important buyer protection. Title and capacity claims are typically the highest-value items and should carry the broadest exposure. Collapsing them into the 20%/18-month general regime means the buyer accepts materially less protection on its largest risk category. Worse, tying title to the 18-month window may cut off claims before full dormancy.

**Recommendation.** Refuse. Restore the separate Title regime: 100% cap (or at least preserve seller liability in full for good faith title warranties, capped only at fraud/wilful concealment), and the six-year period. If the Seller objects on administrative simplicity grounds, respond that our deal team's core position is not administratively convenient but protective — this is exactly why we negotiated the carve-out from the outset.

---

## 4. Limitations, Exclusive Remedies & Non-Reliance Applied "to All Claims of Any Nature"

**Playbook position:** Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out of *all* caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance — enforceable to the maximum extent, and no one may waive this.

**Seller position:** Limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

**Assessment.** While the Seller’s language is broadly consistent with the playbook, the **risk** is in implementation: without the fraud carve-out being explicitly stated, the buyer has no assurance it will survive challenge. Our playbook requires the carve-out to be unmistakable. If the Seller's clause simply references "all Claims," a court or mediator reading between the lines could read out the fraud exception. We need to ensure the carved-out categories are explicitly named.

**Recommendation.** Insert an explicit, enumerated fraud/wilful-concealment/deliberate-misconduct carve-out right through the clause. Confirm the Seller has not attempted to narrow or gatekeep these carve-outs. No new evidence needed on our side.

---

## 5. Buyer Knowledge: Blanket Exclusion, Including Data Room and Public Records

**Playbook position:** Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions; qualifier requires named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud, or a specific indemnity.

**Seller position:** Clause 8.3 — Buyer has no claim where Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, *including discoverable from data room or public records*.

**Assessment.** This is a critical departure. The inclusion of "discoverable from data room or public records" effectively insulates the seller from almost any claim that the buyer could reasonably know about — including matters in the very documents the seller should disclose. Combined with a 18-month limitation (see #2 above), this creates a very weak knowledge bar. We have not been given approval to accept anything below 24 months and this clause structurally undermines our position on both dimensions.

**Recommendation.** Delete or heavily qualify the blanket exclusion. Replace with a clause requiring specific fair disclosure (our baseline requirement). If the Seller insists on a knowledge bar, require named seller personnel and a threshold of reasonable diligence — and never let title, capacity, fraud or any specific indemnity fall under it. The disclosure letter does not need an equivalently weak exclusion.

---

## 6. Bluefen Change-Control Consent: Reasonable Endeavours Only

**Playbook position:** Require **effective consent AND evidence** its conditions are satisfied before Completion; reasonable endeavours alone is insufficient for a material customer consent.

**Seller proposal:** Use reasonable endeavours; treat consent as satisfied upon delivery of counterparty's written consent.

**Assessment.** The concern here is temporal sequencing. Our playbook demands the consent and its satisfaction *before* Closing. The Seller's "consent on delivery" approach means the buyer would not get effective consent until some post-closing point, creating a change-control gap during the handover period. Additionally, the seller's statement that the "conditions" in 11.3 have not been confirmed is dangerous — requiring confirmation of conditions is the standard prudent approach.

**Recommendation.** (a) Require the seller to obtain and deliver the Bluefen change-control consent **before** Completion, along with proof that all conditions under 11.3 are satisfied. (b) Require the seller to confirm within a commercially reasonable period after receiving the consent that all conditions are met and not subsequently vary them. (c) Keep this separate from the generic disclosure — the seller must not cite this as a "disclosure."

---

## 7. Riverlark Bank Facility: Post-Completion Release

**Playbook position:** Require current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds and **effective security releases**. A post-completion release needs an **irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval**.

**Seller position:** Release provided following Completion only.

**Assessment.** The Seller’s position mirrors our own requirements except that it lacks the irrevocable undertaking and Amelia Frost gate. With ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding, this is material. The risk is that the release may be delayed, conditional, or poorly executed, leaving the buyer unsecured against the facility during the integration period.

**Recommendation.** Insist the Seller provide: (a) immediate payout from Completion funds; (b) the release executed on Closing, preceded by an irrevocable undertaking; (c) Amelia Frost approval, signed off now, confirming acceptance of the release terms. Do not accept a "release on delivery."

---

## 8. DD-005 Employee Bonuses (AUD 420,000)

**Playbook position:** Must be a **specific line item** in the funds flow, either itemised as seller-funded or included on the Closing balance; the funds-flow mechanism must not silently exclude the amounts.

**Seller says:** DD-005 is recorded but does **not appear** in the draft funds flow, and the disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

**Assessment.** Silent exclusion of AUD 420,000 on completion bonuses is unacceptable. Either the amounts flow through as a specific line item, or the seller must fund them. The seller’s failure to specify tax/super/on-cost treatment creates uncertainty on both sides.

**Recommendation.** Reconstruct the funds flow to include DD-005 with specific identification of bonus amounts, funding source (seller-funded vs. Closing balance), and appropriate tax/super/on-cost breakdown. If the seller cannot produce this cleanly, fund the bonuses via a sellers' escrow account and confirm the completion closing reflects this. Do not leave it ambiguous in the disclosure letter alone.

---

## 9. Ironquay IP Indemnity (AUD 180,000)

**Playbook position:** Broaden the narrow indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 is **not independently verified** either way.

**Seller says:** Existing indemnity limited to specific SOW3 payment; considered adequate.

**Assessment.** The Seller is effectively telling us not to seek more. The playbook's requirement for broadening and for the conclusion that no independent bank verification exists means our risk appetite must tolerate uncertainty but not a seller’s closed-minded assertion that "it’s adequate." At AUD 180,000, depending on what the underlying IP issue is, this may warrant escalation.

**Recommendation.** We do not have current evidence to choose sides on whether broadening is warranted; the DD-010 open balance supports our position that verification remains uncertain. Insist the seller confirm, in writing and on record, that the AUD 180,000 indemnity reflects a complete and verified resolution, and that the SOW3 cure will operate as preserved. Do not concede "adequate" without documentation.

---

## 10. Export/Privacy Incident (DD-006)

**Playbook position:** Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume **no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty, or numeric demand** in either direction.

**Seller says:** Preliminary operational matter; no indication of breach, harm, notification or demand amounts.

**Assessment.** The Seller’s position is broadly aligned with ours — assuming no confirmed breach/harm — but several risks remain: the disclosure characterises it as "may contain" rather than "contained," leaving scope unclear; the 1,240-record dataset could still trigger privacy obligations even without a confirmed breach (e.g., GDPR-style data transfer restrictions); and the lack of investigation updates means we have limited visibility on remediation timelines.

**Recommendation.** Accept the Seller’s no-harm position, but (a) require the seller to maintain and update an investigation log with dates, findings, and timings; (b) agree that the disclosure shall include updates as investigations progress, including potential notification obligations; (c) express concern that a 1,240-record export involving names and business emails could engage data-protection obligations regardless of breach status. Flag for Amelia Frost.

---

## 11. Sandbar Renewals (AUD 330,000 Aggregate)

**Playbook position:** Assess; **no automatic Debt classification** and **no price deduction**; ordinary course is our starting assumption but is not unconditional.

**Seller says:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Assessment.** The Seller treats them as immaterial and harmlessly general. The risk lies in timing — renewals booked just before closing may have rent-default risk, term-renewal options, or tax-timing exposure that the seller attributes to "ordinary course."

**Recommendation.** Request each renewal's specific terms (dates, amounts, trigger events, any break clauses, renewal options, tax-timing provisions). Accept ordinary-course as the default basis, but insist that a classification as “supplier renewals” does not create any indemnity or deemed-debt override. Move the renewal terms from the disclosure letter into the funds-flow schedule for completeness.

---

## 12. Title Evidence: DD-012 Share Register Relied Upon

**Playbook position:** Require **independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence**; DD-012 is a supplied internal source, not independent proof.

**Seller says:** DD-012 identifies Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% shares — the source relied on for title.

**Assessment.** DD-012 alone is insufficient under our position; an independent check (shareholder register, encumbrance register, authority to assign, market register check, and ideally a law firm opinion) is required.

**Recommendation.** Maintain our independent-title position. Add, within the SPA, a requirement that the seller provide independent evidence (encumbrance register, shareholder register, assignment authority, optional third-party opinion) and that the buyer confirm same before Completion. Do not rely solely on the DD-012 share register.

---

## 13. Tax / IP Warranty Positions Settled Under General Regime

**Playbook position:** Tax/IP terms remain **OPEN**; assume no unlimited liability and no resolution.

**Seller says:** Settled under the general regime above.

**Assessment.** This contradicts our open position. Tax and IP warranties are typically among the highest-value matters in an acquisition and should be ring-fenced outside a general cap. Closing tax liabilities is often deferred or structured; IP issues can surface years post-closing. Collapsing them into the general 20%/18-month regime removes buyer protections that our deal team deliberately preserved.

**Recommendation.** Preserve a separate, open-ended tax and IP warranty regime. Do not accept settlement into the general regime. If the seller argues administrative simplicity, hold firm — our deal team deliberately kept these categories open for commercial protection.

---

# Summary Recommendations — Action Items for the Deal Team

| # | Issue | Deal Move |
|---|-------|-----------|
| 1 | 20% cap + de minimis/basket lowered | Push back on de minimis/basket upward; require Amelia Frost pre-auth for 20% |
| 2 | 18-month time limit | Reject; restore 24-month standard; split Title if needed |
| 3 | Title/capacity claims in general regime | Refuse collapse; restore 100%-cap/six-year separate Title regime |
| 4 | Fraud carve-out not explicit | Ensure explicit fraud/wilful-concealment carving-out survives |
| 5 | Blanket buyer-knowledge exclusion incl. data room | Delete; require named seller personnel + reasonable diligence |
| 6 | Bluefen consent on delivery | Require consent + condition evidence BEFORE Completion |
| 7 | Riverlark release post-completion only | Require irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval |
| 8 | DD-005 bonuses not in funds flow | Reconstruct funds flow with specific line item + tax/super breakdown |
|

**Playbook position:** Require current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds and **effective security releases**. A post-completion release needs an **irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval**.

**Seller position:** Release provided following Completion only.

**Assessment.** The Seller’s position mirrors our own requirements except that it lacks the irrevocable undertaking and Amelia Frost gate. With ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding, this is material. The risk is that the release may be delayed, conditional, or poorly executed, leaving the buyer unsecured against the facility during the integration period.

**Recommendation.** Insist the Seller provide: (a) immediate payout from Completion funds; (b) the release executed on Closing, preceded by an irrevocable undertaking; (c) Amelia Frost approval, signed off now, confirming acceptance of the release terms. Do not accept a "release on delivery."

## 8. DD-005 Employee Bonuses (AUD 420,000)

**Playbook position:** Must be a **specific line item** in the funds flow, either itemised as seller-funded or included on the Closing balance; the funds-flow mechanism must not silently exclude the amounts.

**Seller says:** DD-005 is recorded but does **not appear** in the draft funds flow, and the disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

**Assessment.** Silent exclusion of AUD 420,000 on completion bonuses is unacceptable. Either the amounts flow through as a specific line item, or the seller must fund them. The seller’s failure to specify tax/super/on-cost treatment creates uncertainty on both sides.

**Recommendation.** Reconstruct the funds flow to include DD-005 with specific identification of bonus amounts, funding source (seller-funded vs. Closing balance), and appropriate tax/super/on-cost breakdown. If the seller cannot produce this cleanly, fund the bonuses via a sellers' escrow account and confirm the completion closing reflects this. Do not leave it ambiguous in the disclosure letter alone.

## 9. Ironquay IP Indemnity (AUD 180,000)

**Playbook position:** Broaden the narrow indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 is **not independently verified** either way.

**Seller says:** Existing indemnity limited to specific SOW3 payment; considered adequate.

**Assessment.** The Seller is effectively telling us not to seek more. The playbook's requirement for broadening and for the conclusion that no independent bank verification exists means our risk appetite must tolerate uncertainty but not a seller’s closed-minded assertion that "it’s adequate." At AUD 180,000, depending on what the underlying IP issue is, this may warrant escalation.

**Recommendation.** We do not have current evidence to choose sides on whether broadening is warranted; the DD-010 open balance supports our position that verification remains uncertain. Insist the seller confirm, in writing and on record, that the AUD 180,000 indemnity reflects a complete and verified resolution, and that the SOW3 cure will operate as preserved. Do not concede "adequate" without documentation.

## 10. Export/Privacy Incident (DD-006)

**Playbook position:** Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume **no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty, or numeric demand** in either direction.

**Seller says:** Preliminary operational matter; no indication of breach, harm, notification or demand amounts.

**Assessment.** The Seller’s position is broadly aligned with ours — assuming no confirmed breach/harm — but several risks remain: the disclosure characterises it as "may contain" rather than "contained," leaving scope unclear; the 1,240-record dataset could still trigger privacy obligations even without a confirmed breach (e.g., GDPR-style data transfer restrictions); and the lack of investigation updates means we have limited visibility on remediation timelines.

**Recommendation.** Accept the Seller’s no-harm position, but (a) require the seller to maintain and update an investigation log with dates, findings, and timings; (b) agree that the disclosure shall include updates as investigations progress, including potential notification obligations; (c) express concern that a 1,240-record export involving names and business emails could engage data-protection obligations regardless of breach status. Flag for Amelia Frost.

## 11. Sandbar Renewals (AUD 330,000 Aggregate)

**Playbook position:** Assess; **no automatic Debt classification** and **no price deduction**; ordinary course is our starting assumption but is not unconditional.

**Seller says:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Assessment.** The Seller treats them as immaterial and harmlessly general. The risk lies in timing — renewals booked just before closing may have rent-default risk, term-renewal options, or tax-timing exposure that the seller attributes to "ordinary course."

**Recommendation.** Request each renewal's specific terms (dates, amounts, trigger events, any break clauses, renewal options, tax-timing provisions). Accept ordinary-course as the default basis, but insist that a classification as “supplier renewals” does not create any indemnity or deemed-debt override. Move the renewal terms from the disclosure letter into the funds-flow schedule for completeness.

## 12. Title Evidence: DD-012 Share Register Relied Upon

**Playbook position:** Require **independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence**; DD-012 is a supplied internal source, not independent proof.

**Seller says:** DD-012 identifies Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% shares — the source relied on for title.

**Assessment.** DD-012 alone is insufficient under our position; an independent check (shareholder register, encumbrance register, authority to assign, market register check, and ideally a law firm opinion) is required.

**Recommendation.** Maintain our independent-title position. Add, within the SPA, a requirement that the seller provide independent evidence (encumbrance register, shareholder register, assignment authority, optional third-party opinion) and that the buyer confirm same before Completion. Do not rely solely on the DD-012 share register.

## 13. Tax / IP Warranty Positions Settled Under General Regime

**Playbook position:** Tax/IP terms remain **OPEN**; assume no unlimited liability and no resolution.

**Seller says:** Settled under the general regime above.

**Assessment.** This contradicts our open position. Tax and IP warranties are typically among the highest-value matters in an acquisition and should be ring-fenced outside a general cap. Closing tax liabilities is often deferred or structured; IP issues can surface years post-closing. Collapsing them into the general 20%/18-month regime removes buyer protections that our deal team deliberately preserved.

**Recommendation.** Preserve a separate, open-ended tax and IP warranty regime. Do not accept settlement into the general regime. If the seller argues administrative simplicity, hold firm — our deal team deliberately kept these categories open for commercial protection.
